For the cyclic, orientation-preserving action under consideration, one needs local classification of periodic surface homeomorphisms, a conformal structure on the quotient with its branch data, and its lift to the source. The local classification also explains why a nontrivial orientation-preserving periodic map has isolated fixed points, whereas an orientation-reversing involution can fix a curve (Constantin & Kolev, 1994, Lemma 2.5 and the disc theorem). Nielsen realization addresses the different problem of realizing an abstract finite subgroup of the mapping class group and should not replace this step without explaining the passage from the given action.

After triviality of the induced linear action has been established, the remaining automorphism of the degree-one generalized-Jacobian torsor is a translation, and the manuscript still needs a proof that a nonzero translation cannot preserve the embedded hyperbolic curve. The application only needs the finite-order case: a nonzero torsion translation acts freely, and the Abel map identifies ordinary first homology through the compact-Jacobian quotient and the peripheral torus kernel. Translation therefore acts trivially on that homology, and the transfer/Euler-characteristic argument of N007.6 excludes it. This proof route requires the stated homology comparison, rather than following from the embedding property alone.

For a connected orientable surface \(X\) of finite type with \(\chi(X)<0\), start with a nontrivial finite-order orientation-preserving map acting trivially on \(H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\), replace it by a nonidentity power of prime order \(p\), and remove its finite fixed-point set, so the resulting \(C_p\)-action on \(V\) is free. In the homology exact sequence for deleting those points, the old homology and the new peripheral kernel are fixed, hence the finite-order action on their extension is trivial over \(\mathbb Q\), and then over torsion-free integral first homology. Transfer identifies the quotient's rational first homology with the invariants, so source and quotient have equal first Betti numbers and equal Euler characteristics because they are simultaneously compact or noncompact; multiplicativity \(\chi(V)=p\chi(V/C_p)<0\) is then impossible. This repairs the reduction without a relative-isotopy assertion, with finiteness of the fixed set obtained by extending the periodic map over the finite-puncture compactification and applying the local periodic-map classification there (Constantin & Kolev, 1994).

For a closed orientable genus-two surface \(X\), the hyperelliptic mapping class generates a subgroup of order two, but no unramified covering of that surface onto a closed orientable target can have a deck group containing an involution: the resulting free involution would give \(-2=2\chi(X/C_2)\), hence \(\chi(X/C_2)=-1\), impossible for a closed orientable quotient. Thus the NB is too strong for the finite étale arrows actually defined here, even before considering orientation-reversing mapping classes. Nielsen realization provides finite isometry actions, which may have fixed points; orbifold quotients or removal of the fixed points would change the category (Kerckhoff, 1980, Theorem 1; 1983).

For a covering orbit with finite deck stabilizer \(D\subset\mathcal T_X\), the proposed balanced product is modeled by the corresponding quotient of \(\widehat{\mathcal T}_X\) by the image of \(D\), which is closed because it is finite. To preserve the original stabilizer faithfully, one must also know that \(D\to\widehat{\mathcal T}_X\) is injective, the issue singled out on 014. This special situation is substantially better behaved than the general categorical construction on 012, where stabilizers may be infinite and nonclosed in their profinite images.

### N060.1 — Boundary pinnings point toward tangential base points and cyclotomic inertia

For a smooth curve over a characteristic-zero field, replace a topological boundary direction by a nonzero tangent vector at a rational puncture and use the tangential fiber functor, so peripheral monodromy becomes a based map \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)\to\pi_1^{\mathrm{ét}}\). At such a rational tangential base point, the local parameter covers \(z\mapsto z^n\) show that Galois acts on inertia through the cyclotomic character; comparison with an interior base point introduces the path cocycle of 070. This gives a concrete bridge from the stated monodromy motivation to the subsequent Galois-groupoid section, but a real ray alone is not a rational tangent vector and the arithmetic datum must be supplied. Confidence is high for this bridge in the smooth-curve case, using Deligne's construction (1989, §§15.13–15.18); no novelty is asserted.
### N067.2 — Passing to Qᵃᵇ removes the cyclotomic character but not all path information

Every root of unity lies in \(\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}\), so the cyclotomic character becomes trivial over that base, but a path torsor may still be nontrivial. For example, the cube-root torsor of 2 is not trivial over \(\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}\): a cube root of 2 would generate a non-Galois extension of \(\mathbb Q\), whereas every finite subextension of an abelian Galois extension is Galois. Thus even a Kummer path torsor on \(\mathbb G_m\) can retain arithmetic information after the local inertia character is made constant. The “limit” language can be made precise for finite étale covers by descent along the directed union of number fields, with compatibility of morphisms and fibers included (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.14.1).
### N069.1 — A cyclotomic example proves that the topological path subgroupoid need not be stable

Take \(X=\mathbb G_m/\mathbb Q\) based at 1, where the comparison sends \(\mathbb Z\) into \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)\), and the finite covers \(z\mapsto z^n\) make Galois act by the cyclotomic character. Choose \(u\) whose character \(\chi(u)\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}\) is neither 1 nor −1; such cyclotomic automorphisms exist and extend to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) and then to \(\mathbb C\). The topological generator 1 maps to \(\chi(u)\), which is not an ordinary integer because \(\mathbb Z\cap\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}=\{1,-1\}\). This gives a concrete obstruction independently of the noncontinuity of a field automorphism on complex points; the finite-cover description is also recorded by Deligne (1989, §14.2).

### N067.2 — Passing to Qᵃᵇ removes the cyclotomic character but not all path information

Every root of unity lies in \(\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}\), so the cyclotomic character becomes trivial over that base, but a path torsor may still be nontrivial. For example, the cube-root torsor of 2 is not trivial over \(\mathbb Q^{\mathrm{ab}}\): a cube root of 2 would generate a non-Galois extension of \(\mathbb Q\), whereas every finite subextension of an abelian Galois extension is Galois. Thus even a Kummer path torsor on \(\mathbb G_m\) can retain arithmetic information after the local inertia character is made constant. The “limit” language can be made precise for finite étale covers by descent along the directed union of number fields, with compatibility of morphisms and fibers included (The Stacks Project Authors, n.d., Lemma 58.14.1).

After compactifying the ends, trivial action on ordinary integral homology forces the punctures to be fixed individually and makes the compact-surface Lefschetz number \(2-2g\); a nontrivial orientation-preserving periodic map has isolated fixed points of index \(+1\), by its local rotation model. For a connected orientable surface \(X\) of finite type with \(\chi(X)<0\), start with a nontrivial finite-order orientation-preserving map acting trivially on \(H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\), replace it by a nonidentity power of prime order \(p\), and remove its finite fixed-point set, so the resulting \(C_p\)-action on \(V\) is free. In the homology exact sequence for deleting those points, the old homology and the new peripheral kernel are fixed, hence the finite-order action on their extension is trivial over \(\mathbb Q\), and then over torsion-free integral first homology. Transfer identifies the quotient's rational first homology with the invariants, so source and quotient have equal first Betti numbers and equal Euler characteristics because they are simultaneously compact or noncompact; multiplicativity \(\chi(V)=p\chi(V/C_p)<0\) is then impossible. This repairs the reduction without a relative-isotopy assertion, with finiteness of the fixed set obtained by extending the periodic map over the finite-puncture compactification and applying the local periodic-map classification there (Constantin & Kolev, 1994).

The proposition claims geometric connectedness of the boundary in every fibre when $\dim M_G\geq2$, and scans 073–075 provide a combinatorial proof strategy. To complete that strategy over the stated base, one must establish geometric connectedness of the component moduli factors and realize the required graph incidences in every geometric fibre. Deligne and Mumford (1969, Theorem 5.2) provide the normal-crossing boundary framework for their stable-curve stacks, while Keel (1992, Catalogue, Facts 1–4) makes the genus-zero boundary products and intersections explicit; neither citation by itself substitutes for checking the precise marked products used here.

For this finite union of connected boundary divisors, the proposed argument is equivalently the connectedness of the graph joining two divisors when their intersection is nonempty. In genus zero, the edges of this incidence graph can be checked using compatibility of the two marking partitions (Keel, 1992, Catalogue, Fact 4). This proves a statement about connected components; the later fundamental-groupoid programme additionally needs relations among paths, which are not encoded by that incidence graph alone.

An adjacent exchange of markings produces two maximal chains whose common edge contraction has a four-pointed rational component. The proof is completed by the connected one-dimensional family of that component and its boundary degenerations, which stays inside the ambient boundary because other nodes remain in the range under consideration; the relevant boundary product descriptions are explicit in Keel (1992, Catalogue, Facts 2–4). Generating all permutations by adjacent exchanges then gives the claimed connectivity, while relations among those exchanges remain a separate issue for the programme beginning on scan 076.
**Checked scope:** Catalogue, Facts 1–4, pp. 551–553: genus-zero boundary products and intersection compatibility.
